newsitem.title: USA: Controversies hit Rep. Kennedy's political hopes.
newsitem.headline: Controversies hit Rep. Kennedy's political hopes.

text.p: Representative Joseph Kennedy, whose political aspirations have been hit by family controversies, including allegations his brother had an affair with a 14-year old babysitter, said on Monday the Kennedys had problems like all families.

"Life sometimes is a bit of a struggle for everybody, and our family is no different from any other," said Kennedy, the son of slain Senator Robert Kennedy. "It just gets a little more attention I guess, as you can kind of see," he told reporters.
Kennedy, who publicly apologised last week for mistakes he made during his first marriage, has been slipping in polls ahead of his expected bid for the Massachusetts governorship.
The Boston Globe, quoting unnamed sources, reported on Friday that his brother, Michael Kennedy, had had an affair with his children's 14-year old babysitter.

Michael Kennedy's office has not returned phone calls seeking comment. An attorney for Kennedy, Thomas Dwyer, said in a statement last week: "Because this matter is now under legal review, we will have no comment at this time."
Joseph Kennedy's first wife, Sheila Rauch Kennedy, is on a national tour to promote her book, "Shattered Faith," about her opposition to the annulment of their marriage last October.
The District Attorney in Norfolk County, where Michael Kennedy lives, said on Friday his office will conduct a "preliminary review" of the allegations against him.
A preliminary review is not necessarily a full criminal investigation and whether it becomes one depends on the inquiry.
Under Massachusetts law, sexual relations with a minor under 16 years old is considered statutory rape.

"It's a big family, there's always going to be a few little problems along the way," Joseph Kennedy, a six-term Democratic congressman, said, adding, "and this one might not be such a little one for everybody."
The departure of Massachusetts Governoe William Weld, expected to be named ambassador to Mexico, would have removed Representative Kennedy's biggest barrier to claiming the governor's seat.

Boston Herald polls released last week showed that 61 percent of Massachusetts voters believed the Republican governor should run for a third term, and that he would easily beat Kennedy, a Democrat, in a matchup.

The surveys, taken before the allegations against Michael Kennedy surfaced, showed Joseph Kennedy would beat other prominent Republicans in a gubernatorial race, but his popularity was tarnished by the annulment flap, slipping to 49 percent, down from 66 percent last fall.
"I think if I have another week like this in politics, I'm going to apply for the job in Guatemala," he said.
